<p class="eyebrow">Research questions, contributions, and methods</p>
<p class="lede">My research examines two related problems: how predictive models should be updated when data distributions change, and how fitted loss models should be evaluated in the extreme tail. The studies below distinguish model performance from the decisions made using model estimates.</p>

## Beyond Quantile Agreement: Decomposing Expected Shortfall Discrepancies in Fire-Loss Models {#fire-loss}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil, Shudeshna Nandy, Clement Ampong, Prakash Karki, and Chi-Kuang Yeh</p>

Agreement between a fitted model and empirical high-loss quantiles does not imply agreement in expected tail losses. This study develops a diagnostic framework for identifying where a fitted extreme-loss model and an empirical loss distribution differ.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

The analysis connects an Expected Shortfall discrepancy to comparisons within bounded insurance layers. Established stop-loss identities motivate the decomposition; the contribution is the diagnostic framework for detecting and localizing discrepancies, with inferential procedures for comparisons made using the same data for model fitting and empirical estimation. Detection and localization are assessed as distinct tasks.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and application</summary>

The study uses Peaks-Over-Threshold and Generalized Pareto modeling, bounded-layer expectations, simulation, and uncertainty assessment. Its empirical application considers structure-fire losses recorded in the 2016–2025 U.S. National Fire Incident Reporting System releases. Particular attention is given to sparse extreme observations and the influence of exceptionally large incidents.

</details>

## Selection Regret in Credit-Risk Model Updating Under Distribution Shift: The Role of Recent Labeled Information {#selection-regret}

This study asks whether selecting the oracle updating policy more frequently necessarily reduces the predictive cost of selection mistakes. It examines how the amount of recent labeled information affects decisions to retain, recalibrate, or refit a credit-risk model.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

The study distinguishes the probability of choosing the best fitted candidate from the regret associated with choosing another candidate. Its central finding is that an updating rule can have lower mean selection regret without selecting the oracle policy more frequently. Selection frequency alone is therefore an incomplete measure of decision quality.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and evidence</summary>

Simulation experiments compare model-updating choices under different shift conditions and adaptation-sample sizes. Stratified cross-validation is used for policy selection, and independent evaluation data are used to measure predictive loss. A historical mortgage-data application provides an additional comparison. Results are interpreted in terms of fitted-candidate regret rather than an unattainable population oracle.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Credit risk</span><span>Selection regret</span><span>Validation</span><span>Distribution shift</span></div>
:::

## Predictive Stability and Adaptation Under Distribution Shift: Calibration, Discrimination, and Decision Thresholds in Credit-Risk Modeling {#distribution-shift}

<p class="authors">Silas Bambil and Shudeshna Nandy</p>

This study considers how changes in a deployment population affect probability predictions and the decisions based on them. It compares model retention, recalibration, and refitting across distinct mechanisms of distribution shift.

::: {.finding}
**Research contribution**

The analysis separates calibration, discrimination, and decision-threshold performance, which need not change together. It examines when more limited updates are adequate and when refitting offers an advantage, while distinguishing the choice of an updating policy from its subsequent evaluation.
:::

<details class="methods"><summary>Study design and methods</summary>

The work uses controlled Monte Carlo experiments and mortgage-credit data. Shift scenarios include baseline-risk changes, covariate shift with model misspecification, and changes in predictor effects. Comparisons use separately defined development, validation, and evaluation data.

</details>

<div class="tags"><span>Calibration</span><span>Predictive stability</span><span>Logistic regression</span><span>Model updating</span></div>
